The camera rests on the bare concrete floor of a windowless council archive basement, tilted almost straight up through a 14mm rectilinear lens at f/11, so the scuffed floor and a spilled cardboard box fill the bottom of the frame and the verticals rush inward toward the top. Five gang members stand in a loose arc at the base of one towering column of loose A4 paper, so tall it runs out of the top of the portrait frame; their chins are lifted and their masked faces angled upward, in sage, rust, navy, charcoal and mustard knit, wearing a grey hoodie, a black puffer jacket, a hi-vis orange vest over a fleece, a navy work coat and a padded bomber, with work boots and trainers. Long rows of galvanised steel shelving packed with box files close in on both sides like canyon walls. The only light comes from bare fluorescent tubes on the ceiling far above, one of them stuttering, casting a cold greenish white that flattens the clothes into shadow while the stitched white rings and red triangles glow out of the gloom. A plain printed label stuck to the side of the paper column, bold black capitals, reads THE RULES. Everything from the floor grit to the last visible sheet is sharp, so the stack seems to go on forever; documentary realism, fine digital grain, a slight greenish cast in the shadows.

Five of them stand in a slack single-file queue across a cramped reception room in a tired British town-hall office at lunchtime, facing the counter as if their number is about to be called: one balaclava each in lime green, bubblegum pink, traffic-cone orange, cobalt blue and lemon yellow, worn with a shiny nylon tracksuit, a puffy supermarket anorak, a fleece zipped to the chin, and trainers on a speckled grey carpet. Behind the chipped beige laminate counter, where a bored desk would normally be, a tower of loose and bundled paperwork is wedged floor to ceiling and keeps going, punching up through a missing polystyrene ceiling tile beside a buzzing fluorescent panel; a single sheet of A4 in a curling plastic sleeve is sellotaped to its front, printed in bold black capitals: THE RULES. Around them the room is busy with small sad things: a red take-a-number dispenser on a pole, a rack of sun-bleached leaflets, a row of moulded orange plastic chairs bolted together, a dusty rubber plant, a wall clock, a hand-sanitiser station. Portrait frame, eye level, straight on from about four metres back with a wide 28mm-style lens, deep focus from the front of the queue to the paper, everything sharp. Lit by a single harsh flash fired from the camera into the midday room: flat frontal light, hard thin shadows hugging each figure and the counter edge, glossy hot spots on the laminate and the nylon, the background slightly darker than the subjects. Colour is loud and over-ripe, as on cheap colour negative film from a seaside snapshot, the masks fizzing against the nicotine beige walls and grey carpet. Nobody strikes a pose; they just wait. Deadpan, documentary, faintly ridiculous.

A hushed, elaborately staged photograph in tall portrait format: a quiet residential road in an English town, two facing rows of brick terraces with bay windows and chimney stacks, just after sunset when the sky has gone a deep inky cobalt but every lamp is already burning. Dead centre on the road, blocking it kerb to kerb, towers a monstrous ream of plain office paper, thousands of sheets squared into one pale column that climbs past the gutters and up level with the chimney pots; along the thick edge of its top sheets, stencilled in bold black letters, the words "THE RULES". Down at the foot of the picture, tiny against it, a handful of masked figures in present-day clothes, a padded gilet, a grey hoodie under a bomber, a waterproof cagoule, joggers and white trainers, stand scattered across the road in a ragged line, shoulders back and chins lifted, gazing up the paper cliff; each mask is knitted in its own dull shade, olive, navy, rust, charcoal. The street around them is ordinary and precise: blue and grey recycling bins along the pavement, a dented estate car and a little hatchback nosed against the kerb, a for-sale board, a lamp lit behind thin curtains in nearly every front room. Lighting is plotted like a film set: sodium streetlamps throw orange cones onto damp asphalt, upstairs windows glow honey yellow, a porch light spills across one doorstep, and a single harsh white spotlight, hidden low behind the figures, rakes upward across the face of the paper so its layered edges catch like the strata of a cliff and the lettering stands out crisp. Cool blue above, warm amber below, faint haze hanging over the road. Shot on a large-format camera on a tripod at standing eye height, wide lens looking straight along the road, everything from the bins to the rooftops in deep focus, the paper column tack sharp, utterly still, silent and uncanny.

Here we are inches from one of them: a portrait-format close-up taken from just beside their left shoulder, so the head turns three-quarters toward us with its left cheek nearest, and that red triangle reads clearly, high and off to one side inside the white ring, not centred. Their chin is lifted and the whole head leans back, as though craning to take in something far too tall to see in one look. Charcoal wool in a heavy rib, each loop and loose fibre sharp where the focus falls; the stitched ring sits proud like a thick cord. A dark knitted glove grips the cord collar of an olive waxed-cotton field jacket, ordinary present-day British outdoor wear. Lens: 85mm, aperture open to f/1.8, so only the knit around the triangle is crisp and everything else softens within a hand's width. Low autumn sun pours through an unseen sash window on the left, a slanting band of honey-coloured light raking across the mask so every rib throws a tiny shadow, while the far side of the head sinks into gentle dusk. Above and behind, crowding the upper half, rises a vast blurred cliff of stacked paper reams and loose sheets; on one sheet near its summit, bigger than its neighbours, heavy black print spells THE RULES, out of focus yet legible, the only lettering anywhere. Warm amber and honey on wool and jacket, set against a cool bluish paper white beyond; fine natural grain, matte, unretouched, no bloom.

Tall portrait frame, a straight-down bird's-eye view at night from the summit of an enormous tower of stacked paper in an empty warehouse, so the lens hangs over the edge of a sheer white cliff of page edges that drops away and tapers sharply towards a wet concrete floor far beneath. Right against the lens at the bottom of the frame lies the uppermost page, its fibres sharp, printed with THE RULES in heavy black capitals, the only thing perfectly in focus. Down at the base of that drop, tiny and a little blurred by the depth, four figures in everyday present-day British gear (a puffer coat, a hi-vis vest over a hoodie, a black bomber, a waterproof cagoule, worn trainers) tip their heads right back to stare up into the camera; their wool hoods come in four muted night colours, bottle green, navy, oxblood and charcoal. Three hold small torches pointed straight up the paper face, throwing narrow white shafts that rake across the page edges and catch the stitched ring and red triangle on every hood. Apart from those beams there is just a weak amber streetlamp glow leaking through a grimy window high up the wall, reflected in a puddle by their feet. Everything else falls away into deep black; very wide lens with steep converging lines, a huge gulf of depth between the page and the floor, fine film grain, clean dry air. The paper looms and looks down on them, the drop felt from the wrong side.

Inside an infinity cove painted pure white, where floor bends into back wall along a soft invisible curve, the space reads as limitless and almost weightless. Dead centre rises one sheer column of stacked printer paper, perfectly squared like a sculpture on display, climbing high toward the top edge of this tall vertical picture; its sides show faint hairline layers of sheets. Propped at its base is a modest museum-style caption card printed in small tidy black capitals: THE RULES. Four masked figures wait in an orderly line some distance before the column, backs partly towards us, heads tipped right back to gaze up at it, each face turned a little so the mask front is half visible. Each knitted balaclava is a different vivid hue, tangerine, ultramarine, magenta and lime, every one bearing its white ring and red triangle; from the neck down they are dressed in plain current-day streetwear in black and slate grey, a padded jacket, a fleece, a cagoule, joggers, dark trainers, black gloves. Shot from far back with a long lens, camera at standing eye level, dead level and motionless, strict bilateral symmetry, lots of blank white headroom above the column. Light floods evenly from everywhere so nothing casts a shadow except a whisper of grey under feet and paper; whites are bright, near blown out, yet the wool keeps its texture. Colour scheme: white on white with graphite clothing; the masks and their small red triangles are the sole saturated notes in the whole image. Clean, precise, art-catalogue realism, tactile knit and paper grain.
